profile.name: Mateusz Ciszek
profile.bio: I build software with C# and .NET, from web applications and real-time dashboards to Unity gameplay systems and editor tools. My projects also include Android applications and connected-device interfaces. I focus on modular architecture, clear interfaces, and reusable code that is easy to maintain and extend.

projects.title: SmartBotAPI
projects.summary: A real-time robotics platform connecting an ESP32-C3 tracked robot to a Blazor dashboard for remote driving, depth visualization, and telemetry history.
projects.imageAlt: SmartBot tracked robot during a corridor driving test
overview: Developed in 2024–2025, SmartBotAPI connects a physical ESP32-C3 robot to an authenticated web interface. With the robot and server online and the server reachable over the internet, an authorized operator can control the robot remotely from anywhere with an internet connection, using a joystick or keyboard.

The robot streams an 8×8 time-of-flight depth map, 6-axis IMU data, and temperature over a secure WebSocket/SignalR channel. Measurements are persisted to SQL Server and visualized as live heatmaps, interpolated depth matrices, and historical charts.
The system was demonstrated using Azure App Service, but that deployment is no longer hosted. The recordings below show the project in action.

sections.title: System Overview
paragraphs: Robot: the VL53L5CX depth sensor and MPU6050 IMU connect to the ESP32-C3 over I²C. The controller drives the motors through a TB6612FNG using PWM.
Server: ASP.NET Core hosts the /signalhub SignalR hub. Incoming telemetry feeds the depth visualizations and a measurement service backed by SQL Server.
Dashboard: authenticated Blazor pages exchange live data and movement commands with the hub. Sensor data travels from robot to dashboard; control commands travel back to the robot.

image.alt: Sensors feed the ESP32-C3, which drives the motors and exchanges SignalR messages with the ASP.NET Core server. The server supplies depth views, stores telemetry in SQL Server, and connects to the authenticated Blazor dashboard.

sections.title: LIDAR / ToF obstacle detection
paragraphs: Obstacle-detection and movement-stop algorithm demonstrated in the video. The VL53L5CX is an 8×8 multizone time-of-flight depth sensor: it measures nearby surfaces in front of the robot to support local obstacle awareness, rather than global positioning or autonomous mapping.

The firmware samples depth at 15 Hz and evaluates the average distance in the central 4×4 region. When that distance drops below 400 mm, it inhibits forward movement to reduce the risk of a collision, while allowing the operator to reverse away. This is a proximity guard, not a guarantee of collision avoidance in every situation.

links.label: Watch web steering and obstacle detection

sections.title: Features
paragraphs: Remote driving — proportional joystick and arrow-key controls send independent motor PWM commands, with two gauges showing commanded motor output.
Live depth visualization — an 8×8 sensor frame is rendered as a heatmap and bilinearly interpolated into a 32×32 matrix.
Telemetry history — date-filtered charts show temperature, average distance, acceleration, and rotation, backed by SQL Server.

Firmware safeguards — a 700 ms command timeout stops the motors, and a proximity guard inhibits forward movement near obstacles. The firmware supports fallback Wi-Fi networks and reconnects its WebSocket connection.
Authenticated access — dashboard operators use ASP.NET Core Identity; the robot uses a separate API key. Production communication uses TLS/WSS.
Deployment support — Docker packaging and GitHub Actions provide build, test, and artifact workflows. Azure App Service was used for the presentation deployment.

sections.title: One-joystick differential drive and keyboard input
paragraphs: JoystickInputHandler converts on-screen input into proportional throttle and steering, with positive y representing forward motion. A center dead zone prevents accidental movement, while a steering dead zone keeps near-vertical input moving straight. Outside these zones, the controller continuously mixes both axes rather than snapping to the direction shown by the UI label.
sections.codeCaption: Equal motor values drive straight; unequal values create a curve; opposite values at y = 0 rotate the robot in place. PWM ranges from −255 to +255: the sign selects direction and the magnitude sets duty cycle.
sections.tableCaption: keyboardInputHandler provides a discrete fallback using the same motor-command contract.
afterTableParagraphs: The dashboard continuously samples the held joystick and throttles outgoing SignalR commands to one every 250 ms. Releasing the pointer or key sends (0, 0) immediately. The firmware independently clamps received values and stops both motors after 700 ms without a command, providing an automatic stop if browser or network control is lost.

sections.title: Remote control and live depth
paragraphs: SignalR carries telemetry toward the dashboard and motor commands back to the robot. An 8×8 ToF depth frame is displayed as a heatmap and an interpolated 32×32 matrix. SQL Server stores measurements for historical charts.

projects.title: Smart City Hub
projects.summary: An IoT platform connecting a React dashboard, Node.js API, and ESP32 modules to control a physical LEGO city.
projects.imageAlt: Illuminated LEGO city model used to demonstrate Smart City Hub
overview: Developed in 2024 and demonstrated at the KI AT student club, Smart City Hub connects a physical LEGO city to a web-based monitoring and control system. It combines ESP32-based IoT devices, a central Node.js/TypeScript API, and a React web dashboard.
The web dashboard and ESP32 firmware share a Node.js/MongoDB API for device control, sensor readings, and state history.

sections.title: Web dashboard and authentication
paragraphs: JWT login separates administrator and user access. Administrators manage accounts and devices; users control their assigned devices.

sections.title: Architecture
paragraphs: The React dashboard communicates with the Express/TypeScript API over REST with JWT authentication. ESP32 polls the API for output states, while Mongoose connects the backend to MongoDB.

image.alt: React web dashboard and ESP32 communicate with the Express TypeScript API, which connects to MongoDB through Mongoose.

sections.caption: Architecture Diagram of the Smart City Hub

sections.title: Features
paragraphs: Device control — up to 96 digital outputs (6 MCP23017 expanders × 16 pins) controlled remotely from the web dashboard; the ESP32 periodically polls the API for states and drives the outputs.
Sensor readings — temperature, pressure, and humidity stored in the database with a reading date and device ID.
Roles and authentication — JWT login with separate admin / user roles; admins manage users and devices, users control their assigned devices.
State history — every device keeps a timestamped on/off history.

projects.title: Bonnie's Farmville
projects.summary: A Unity farming-economy minigame for the upcoming Nintendo Switch 2 title 40in1 GameCollection Vol3, featuring a data-driven farming grid and autonomous companion AI.
projects.imageAlt: Bonnie's Farmville title artwork featuring a rabbit with a watering can, vegetable plots, and farm animals
overview: Bonnie's Farmville connects a data-driven world grid with autonomous companion AI. Gameplay configuration is separated from runtime logic, so new farm layouts, crops, items, prices, and upgrades can be authored without rewriting the underlying systems.

screenshots.alt: Bonnie and a companion beside growing crops and the inventory toolbar.
Crop shop showing seed prices, buy/sell tabs, and the player's inventory.
Upgrade shop with tool levels and an unlockable bunny companion.
End-of-run statistics showing crop quantities and their total value.
Bonnie and a companion among planted seeds, growing crops, and mature berry plants.
Watering a farm plot with a bunny companion nearby.

sections.title: Data-driven farming grid
sections.summary: A reusable authoring pipeline that turns visual tile painting into structured runtime data for farming interactions and navigation.
paragraphs: I created a tile-based data layer that converts painted Unity Tilemaps into reusable gameplay properties for individual grid cells. Designers can mark diggable areas, walkable paths, water sources, placement zones, and NPC obstacles directly in the Scene view. An editor component collects these layers into a serialized ScriptableObject containing the coordinates and property values used at runtime.

The runtime grid manager translates between world and cell coordinates, combines multiple properties for each cell, validates player actions, and stores temporary state such as dug soil, watering, planted seeds, and crop growth. The same data source is shared with other systems.

image.alt: Painted Diggable tiles, the grid authoring component, and the serialized grid-property list in Unity

sections.caption: Painted tilemap layers are converted into a serialized per-cell property list used by gameplay systems at runtime.

additionalImages.alt: Grid Manager converts authored ScriptableObject data into a coordinate-keyed runtime dictionary for digging, watering, planting, and pathfinding

sections.title: Companion AI and pathfinding
sections.summary: Lightweight companion behaviour combining authored navigation data, A* routing, movement states, avoidance, and recovery logic.
paragraphs: I developed an unlockable companion system with grid-aware A* pathfinding. Pets roam near the player, begin following when the distance becomes too large, and stop at a comfortable range instead of overlapping the character. Their movement queries the same walkability and obstacle data used by the farming grid.

The behaviour includes safe spawn selection, player avoidance, directional animation, idle timing, failed-path handling, and teleport recovery when the companion is separated by an extreme distance. Paths are calculated only when a new destination is selected, avoiding unnecessary searches every frame while still responding to player movement.

image.alt: In-game companion beside the player, paired with the NPC obstacle tilemap and serialized grid data in Unity

sections.caption: The companion uses the authored Path and obstacle layers for A* navigation while roaming near and following the player.

sections.title: Item and crop definitions
sections.summary: Shared ScriptableObject definitions connect inventory, shops, crops, and progression.
paragraphs: I built a shared item-data pipeline that drives inventory limits, seed prices, crop rewards, tool tiers, and shop presentation. Item and crop definitions are stored in ScriptableObjects, making it straightforward to add new items without changing the underlying gameplay systems.

image.alt: Runtime crop shop beside Unity Inspector panels for Item and Crop ScriptableObject configuration

sections.caption: The runtime shop uses shared Item and Crop ScriptableObject definitions for prices, inventory limits, crop rewards, and upgrades.

sections.title: Crop Details Generator
paragraphs: Automatically generates crop definitions from the shared item database, linking seed IDs to harvest rewards, growth times, and growth-stage sprites. Built-in validation identifies missing or invalid crop data directly in the Unity Inspector.

projects.title: Power Washer Hero
projects.summary: A reusable Unity cleaning pipeline with GPU-painted dirt masks, compute-shader coverage tracking, and editor tools for configuring multi-part cleaning targets.
projects.imageAlt: Power Washer Hero title artwork showing a car being pressure-washed in a garage
overview: I built a reusable Unity cleaning pipeline with GPU-painted dirt masks, compute-shader coverage tracking, per-part and overall progression, animated UI feedback, and configurable procedural dirt materials. Editor tools rapidly convert multi-part models into calibrated cleaning targets.

sections.title: GPU-driven washable surfaces
paragraphs: Each washable mesh owns a runtime dirt mask stored in a RenderTexture. The pressure washer projects a world-space brush onto the target, while a custom shader uses surface normals to reject backfaces and prevent the spray from cleaning through corners. Dirt is removed cumulatively, producing persistent, localized cleaning across complex shapes.

image.alt: Power Washer cleaning pipeline showcase with gameplay, Unity material setup, and per-part calibration data

sections.caption: GPU-driven cleaning connects persistent dirt masks, per-part progress, and reusable authoring tools.

sections.title: Real-time coverage measurement
paragraphs: A compute shader reduces the dirt-mask pixels into coverage data. The result is converted into a normalized completion percentage for every individual car part, giving the game accurate progress values without relying on trigger counts or hand-authored checkpoints.

sections.title: Configurable dirt materials
paragraphs: The washable surface shader blends clean albedo with procedural dirt using tunable noise, tint, scale, opacity, smoothness, and metallic controls. This lets one cleaning system support varied materials and grime patterns while preserving the original look of each model.

image.alt: Procedural dirt shader breakdown showing Unity material settings, clean albedo, dirt noise, a runtime paint mask, and the layered result

sections.caption: Clean albedo and procedural dirt are blended through a runtime paint mask, with configurable noise and surface properties.

sections.title: Reachability calibration tool
paragraphs: A generated ScriptableObject stores the maximum realistically cleanable percentage for every mesh part and records the last percentage reached during testing. Designers can compensate for UV seams, hidden geometry, or inaccessible pixels, so a visually clean part can still reach 100% in gameplay.

screenshots.alt: Partially cleaned car with individual part percentages and overall cleaning progress.
A multi-part cleaning target with localized dirt removal and overall progress feedback.
Front view of a car with cleaned patches revealing its paint and windshield beneath the dirt.

projects.title: MaCster Framework
projects.subtitle: Modular Unity Gameplay Systems Library
projects.summary: A reusable, data-driven collection of Unity gameplay systems for dialogue, inventory, commerce, and grid-based construction.
projects.technologies: Unity 6, C#, ScriptableObjects, xNode, Unity UI, custom editor tooling
projects.focusAreas: Gameplay systems, editor tooling, node graphs, data-driven design, UI programming, rapid prototyping
overview: Dialogue — Visual node graphs with branching choices, Boolean conditions, and gameplay action hooks.
Inventory — Item stacks, toolbar slots, container transfers, and configurable chest capacity.
Shops — Category filters, quantity-based carts, and purchase-validation callbacks.
Construction prototype — Socket snapping, placement previews, and occupancy checks.
Reusable tools — ScriptableObject data, Inspector tooling, interaction, JSON saving, and object pooling.

sections.title: From authoring to runtime
sections.summary: Reusable assets hold content; scene components run the systems and present their UI.
paragraphs: The dialogue architecture separates authored content from playback and presentation. Custom nodes describe the conversation, DialoguePlayer decides what happens next, and the viewer renders the active node. This makes the authoring workflow visible in Unity while keeping gameplay actions and conditions extensible.

image.alt: Diagram showing custom xNode dialogue assets, text and response nodes, Boolean conditions, and UnityEvents feeding DialoguePlayer and DialogBoxViewer.

sections.title: Dialogue System
sections.summary: A visual conversation-authoring workflow combining NPC text, player responses, branching paths, reusable Boolean conditions, and custom gameplay action hooks.

image.alt: Unity node graph showing branching dialogue, an action node, and a Boolean condition.
image.caption: Branching graph with response, action, condition, and text nodes.

paragraphs: Visual authoring — The dialogue editor extends xNode with entry, text, player-response, Boolean-condition, and action nodes. Text nodes carry dialogue lines, a speaker name, and a portrait; response nodes generate an output port for each choice so authors can connect distinct conversation paths.

Conditions and gameplay hooks — Boolean conditions are ScriptableObject assets with a Validate() contract. The runtime follows the true or false output automatically, while action nodes invoke UnityEvents that can be wired to gameplay behaviour in the Inspector. DialoguePlayer handles traversal; DialogBoxViewer presents text, portraits, and response buttons through the INodeViewable interface.

sections.title: Inventory System
sections.summary: A shared slot model for player storage, quick-access slots, and chests, with item quantities, stack limits, splitting, merging, and transfers.

gallery.alt: Chest and player inventories displaying stored item quantities.
gallery.caption: Container and player storage.

paragraphs: Item data and slot interactions — SOItemData defines an item’s name, icon, ID, and maximum stack size. InventoryManager connects toolbar, inventory, and chest views to slot data, with a separate mouse-held slot for moving items. Clicking supports pickup, placement, merging matching stacks, and swapping different items.

Item database — SOItemDatabase keeps a shared catalog of SOItemData assets and provides GetItem(id) to retrieve an item by its ID. Its editor-only Set IDs command collects item assets from Resources/ItemData, builds the catalog, and assigns available IDs to items that do not yet have one. Designers can maintain item definitions as reusable assets instead of recreating them for each inventory or chest.

Stack controls and containers — Right-click splitting and mouse-wheel adjustments let the player move part of a stack. Opening a chest supplies its own slot data and shows the appropriate number of container slots.

Events and gameplay integration — Selection and inventory-open events notify subscribed components when the player changes their selected item or opens the inventory. These hooks let gameplay code react to inventory interactions without coupling those reactions to the slot UI, keeping the storage interface reusable across different games.
Sample workflow — The transfer example shows one item in the opened chest and five retained in the player toolbar.

Modular chests — Each InventoryChest component owns its own slot array. Set the Inventory Slot Data size in the Inspector to configure that chest’s capacity; the inventory UI displays the slots supplied by the opened chest. The example below uses seven slots.

sections.title: Shop System
sections.summary: A categorized storefront with item cards, quantity controls, a live cart, and callback-based checks for funds and inventory capacity.

gallery.alt: Shop catalog with category filters and purchasable item cards.
gallery.caption: Category-driven item catalog.

gallery.alt: Shop cart containing multiple item quantities and purchase validation messages.
gallery.caption: Quantity cart and purchase validation.

paragraphs: Catalog and cart — The shop reads item prices and categories through IItemTradeable and IItemType. ShopManager creates catalog cards and category filters from the supplied assets. Adding an item again updates its cart quantity; changing quantities recalculates line prices and the total.

Purchase validation — When the cart changes, separate callbacks check currency and available inventory space. All registered validators must agree. A purchase callback receives the item quantities and total price, and a successful result clears the cart. This keeps the game’s economy and inventory integration outside the storefront UI.

Callback-driven integration — Validation callbacks return whether the transaction is allowed, while the purchase callback delegates the transaction to game-specific code. The storefront manages catalog and cart interactions; the connected game decides how to check funds, verify storage capacity, deduct currency, and deliver items. This separates shop presentation from economy rules and inventory implementation.

Game integration — The included sample uses Inspector-controlled Boolean responses to demonstrate validation and purchase outcomes. It demonstrates the integration hooks; a game supplies the actual currency deduction and item-delivery behaviour.

image.alt: Diagram of shared item assets feeding catalog and cart, then currency and capacity callbacks, and finally a game-supplied purchase handler.

sections.title: Grid Building
sections.summary: An unfinished construction prototype for floor, wall, and door prefabs, with compatible-socket snapping, placement previews, and occupied-socket checks.

gallery.alt: Unity Game view showing a green wall-placement preview on a grid-built room.
gallery.caption: Snapped placement preview.

gallery.alt: Unity Scene view showing the resulting grid-built room layout.
gallery.caption: Generated floor and wall layout.

paragraphs: Snapping and previews — SimpleBuildPlacer casts from the pointer into socket layers, checks which sockets accept the active piece type, and chooses the closest compatible hit. Each socket supplies a placement position and rotation. The preview uses separate valid and ghost materials, and its colliders are disabled.

Placement and prototype scope — Placing a part instantiates the active prefab and records the occupied socket. Floor and wall socket components define compatibility. The supplied revision includes grid-size settings and a grid-rounding helper, but the free-placement branches are disabled; the active placement flow is socket-based. The two videos document unfinished iterations.

sections.title: Supporting tools
sections.summary: Small, reusable utilities support the sample systems and everyday prototyping.
paragraphs: Item authoring — The item database provides an editor context-menu action to collect item assets and assign IDs, with a custom read-only Inspector drawer for generated fields. Item definitions expose stack size, icons, and names as authoring data.
Object pooling — A generic queue-based object pool supports preallocation, reuse, reset hooks, and return-to-pool behaviour.
Save/load persistence — GameSaverManager serializes save data with Newtonsoft.Json to Unity’s persistent data directory.

Player interaction — The interaction module uses camera-directed sphere casts, an IInteractable contract, prompts, and press-versus-hold behaviour. Movement controllers and small UI helpers round out the library.

projects.title: Mobile E-Commerce App
projects.summary: Two Android apps connect customers and store owners through one Firebase-backed shopping workflow.
projects.imageAlt: AI-assisted presentation composite based on the documented customer catalog and owner product editor, connected through Firebase
overview: I developed a two-app mobile store: a customer application for shopping and a dedicated owner application for catalog and order management. The customer flow covers registration, bilingual Polish and English UI, product browsing, cart updates, delivery addresses, checkout, and order history.

The project uses Kotlin activities and fragments, RecyclerView adapters, and a FireStoreClass data-access layer in both apps. Firebase Authentication handles accounts and password reset, Cloud Firestore stores commerce records, and Firebase Storage and Glide handle uploaded images.

sections.title: One backend, two focused apps
sections.summary: Customer and owner interfaces share the same cloud data while keeping their workflows separate.
paragraphs: Both apps use FireStoreClass methods for account data, products, carts, addresses, and orders. RecyclerView adapters display the returned records, while activities and fragments handle navigation, form validation, and UI updates.

projects.title: Unity ML-Agents Pathfinding
projects.summary: A Unity ML-Agents navigation simulation trained with PPO across 20 parallel environments for 500,000 steps, achieving a peak mean reward of 0.951.
projects.imageAlt: Twenty Unity training environments with blue cubes and yellow spheres on red, green, and dark platforms

videos.title: Unity ML-Agents PathFinding - Trained Model In Action v1

overview: This project explores how reinforcement learning can solve a dynamic pathfinding task. I created a Unity training environment in which an autonomous agent moves along the X and Z axes, searches for a randomly placed target, and learns to avoid obstacle walls. Reaching the target gives the agent a +1 reward, while hitting a wall results in a -1 penalty and resets the episode.

To speed up learning, I ran 20 training environments in parallel and trained the agent with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for 500,000 steps. The experiment reached a peak mean reward of 0.951 and maintained a mean reward of approximately 0.9 near the end of training, demonstrating reliable learned navigation.

sections.title: Trained navigation agent
paragraphs: The trained agent navigates around obstacles to reach a target whose position changes between episodes. The platform changes color to show the previous episode's outcome: green means the agent successfully reached the ball, while red means it failed.
